$$\text{ACB}_i = \delta(\text{ACB}_{i-1}, \, e_i) \quad \text{for } i = \tau+1, \dots, t$$

During this folding phase, the supervisor's tool dispatch engine is replaced with a verification interceptor. If the historical log encounters an authorization event $e_{\text{auth}}$ containing an action $a_{\text{ext}}$, the supervisor does not invoke the sandbox RPC client. Instead, it advances its internal program counter and reads the corresponding $e_{\text{obs}}$ record from the log stream, injecting the historical standard output, exit code, or error message directly into the context accumulator.

::: {.column-margin}
**The Escrow Invariant During Replay**
During live execution, memory escrow holds unverified candidate actions until a verification gate passes. During replay, the verification outcome is already known and recorded in the event log. The supervisor's state transition function $\delta$ must still execute the escrow transition logic to ensure that internal state machine assertions—such as token budgets, pending proposal counters, and quota allocations—remain bit-exact across the recovery boundary.
:::

If the supervisor's state transition logic attempts to establish a live network connection or emit an unrecorded tool action during replay, the verification interceptor raises an invariant violation ($A=0$ breach). The presence of any unlogged side effect indicates that the supervisor's code has drifted from the version that authored the trace, or that an unrecorded source of entropy was allowed to influence the live control flow.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example: Recovery Latency and Compute Savings in Trajectory Reconstruction"}
Consider an autonomous coding agent that failed at turn $t = 150$ due to a transient worker node kernel panic. The trajectory maintained an active context window of $L = 48,000$ tokens. The system recorded periodic checkpoints every $K = 50$ turns. The nearest checkpoint was taken at turn $\tau = 100$.

**Physical Parameters:**
- Serialized checkpoint size $|\mathbf{S}_{100}|$: $64\text{ MB}$ (includes serialized ACB, tokenizer cache, and sandbox filesystem overlay metadata).
- NVMe read bandwidth: $3.2\text{ GB/s}$ ($3,200\text{ MB/s}$).
- Event log delta count: $n = 50$ turns ($150$ raw events: 50 model completions, 50 authorizations, 50 observations).
- Average event record size: $4\text{ KB}$ (total event log suffix size: $600\text{ KB}$).
- Supervisor event fold latency: $0.12\text{ ms}$ per event on an AMD EPYC 9654 host processor.
- Upstream inference service characteristics: Frontier model prefill processing rate of $3,000\text{ tokens/s}$ at batch size 1; average decode latency of $25\text{ ms/token}$; average completion length of $200\text{ tokens}$ per turn.

**Trajectory Reconstruction Latency ($T_{\text{recon}}$):**
$$\begin{aligned}
T_{\text{snap\_read}} &= \frac{64\text{ MB}}{3,200\text{ MB/s}} = 0.020\text{ s} = 20.0\text{ ms} \\
T_{\text{log\_read}} &= \frac{0.6\text{ MB}}{3,200\text{ MB/s}} \approx 0.0002\text{ s} = 0.2\text{ ms} \\
T_{\text{event\_fold}} &= 150 \times 0.12\text{ ms} = 18.0\text{ ms} \\
T_{\text{recon}} &= T_{\text{snap\_read}} + T_{\text{log\_read}} + T_{\text{event\_fold}} = 20.0 + 0.2 + 18.0 = 38.2\text{ ms}
\end{aligned}$$

**Hypothetical Stochastic Re-Execution Latency ($T_{\text{re-exec}}$):**
Re-executing the 50 turns through the live model requires recomputing prefill and generating completions across all intermediate turns:
$$\begin{aligned}
T_{\text{prefill\_per\_turn}} &\approx \frac{48,000\text{ tokens}}{3,000\text{ tokens/s}} = 16.0\text{ s} \\
T_{\text{decode\_per\_turn}} &= 200\text{ tokens} \times 0.025\text{ s/token} = 5.0\text{ s} \\
T_{\text{turn\_total}} &= 16.0\text{ s} + 5.0\text{ s} = 21.0\text{ s} \\
T_{\text{re-exec}} &= 50 \times 21.0\text{ s} = 1,050.0\text{ s} \approx 17.5\text{ minutes}
\end{aligned}$$

**Conclusion:**
Deterministic trajectory reconstruction restores the agent control block in $38.2\text{ ms}$, achieving a speedup of:

$$\text{Speedup} = \frac{1,050.0\text{ s}}{0.0382\text{ s}} \approx 27,486\times$$

Reconstruction completely eliminates $17.5$ minutes of GPU idle time, saves tens of dollars in API billing, and introduces zero risk of non-deterministic branching or duplicate environmental side effects.
:::

### Non-Destructive Post-Mortem Debugging

When an autonomous agent exhibits pathological behavior—such as falling into an infinite loop of invalid compiler invocations, exhausting its token budget, or attempting to read unauthorized directories—post-mortem root-cause analysis is exceptionally difficult. In standard software systems, developers inspect core dumps or linear text logs. But text logs from an agent run are deceptive: they reveal what the foundation model produced, but they obscure the internal supervisory control flow, the dynamic context window slicing decisions, and the token budget accounting that triggered the failure.

Brian Kernighan (1979) observed that *"debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place."* When debugging software built around non-deterministic neural components, this difficulty compounds exponentially: if the developer cannot reproduce the exact internal control state, the defect cannot be diagnosed.

Historical trajectory reconstruction provides the foundation for *non-destructive time-travel debugging*. Because the event log records every interaction at the supervisor-model and supervisor-sandbox boundaries, the developer can treat trajectory time as an addressable, scrubbable dimension. A developer can mount an archival trajectory, select any turn $t \in [0, T_{\max}]$, and reconstruct the exact in-memory representation of $\text{ACB}_t$.

```
[Trajectory Timeline: Turns 0 to 48]
Checkpoints:    [S_0]                [S_20]               [S_40]          [Crash: t=48]
                  |                    |                    |                   |
Event Log:       |====E_{0->20}======|====E_{20->40}=====|====E_{40->48}=====|
                  |                    |                    |                   |
Rewind Target:   |                    |           =====>  [Step t=35]          |
                                                    (Load S_20 + Fold 15 events)
```

Time-travel navigation leverages the checkpoint-delta index. To inspect the agent state at turn $t = 35$, the debugger locates the nearest preceding snapshot $\mathbf{S}_{20}$, deserializes the control block, and folds the 15 intervening event pairs from $\mathcal{E}_{20 \to 35}$. The developer can then execute non-destructive diagnostic queries against the reconstructed state:

- **Context Window Slicing Inspection:** The developer inspects the exact token array passed to the model's prefill buffer at step 35. This exposes whether critical prompt instructions, system reminders, or tool documentation were truncated or evicted by the context manager.
- **Dynamic Token Budget Audit:** The developer examines the supervisor's internal token ledger to evaluate whether runaway context growth degraded reasoning performance before the crash occurred.
- **Escrow and Authorization State Review:** The debugger evaluates pending candidate actions $e_{\text{prop}}$ against the active permission mask, revealing whether an overly permissive regex filter allowed a malformed shell argument to escape into the sandbox.
- **Hypothetical Branching (What-If Analysis):** The developer forks the trajectory at turn $t = 35$. The supervisor retains historical state up to turn 35, but switches from replay mode back to live execution under a modified prompt template or corrected tool schema. This allows engineers to verify bug fixes against historical failures without re-running the successful early stages of the task.

### Trace-Driven Regression Testing of Supervisor Logic

A critical challenge in the lifecycle of an agent platform is continuous integration and regression testing. When systems engineers modify the host supervisor—such as optimizing the tool argument parser, refactoring the context compaction algorithm, or updating permission schemas—they must guarantee that these changes do not break existing agent behaviors.

Running live integration test suites against actual foundation model endpoints is impractical for CI pipelines. Foundation model APIs introduce high latency, non-deterministic completions, rate limits, and substantial financial costs. A test that passes in one run may fail in the next solely because the model sampled a rare synonym in a tool parameter, causing flaky test suites that undermine engineering velocity.

Trace-driven regression testing solves this problem by using historical trajectory logs as fixed, golden test vectors. In this harness, the runtime reads hundreds of archived production trajectories and feeds the recorded model completions $e_{\text{prop}}$ directly into the newly modified supervisor logic.

The test harness validates whether the updated supervisor's state transitions match historical invariants. For example, if an engineer rewires the tool call parser to handle streaming JSON tokens, the regression runner replays historical $e_{\text{prop}}$ payloads containing thousands of malformed, escaped, or edge-case tool calls observed in production. The runner asserts that the new parser extracts identical tool names, arguments, and validation errors as the baseline implementation, without invoking a single GPU kernel.

```text
=================================== FAILURES ===================================
_________________ test_supervisor_replay_regression[trace_8492a] ________________
[replay_engine.py:142]: InvariantViolation: Tool argument schema mismatch at turn 14
>   supervisor.apply_event(recorded_event)
E   ValidationError: Tool 'edit_file' argument 'patch' failed validation:
E   Expected valid unified diff string, received unescaped markdown code fence.
E   Historical event e_prop (commit: 9f4a12) accepted this payload via legacy regex fallback.
E   Refactored parser (commit: 3b8c91) rejected payload under strict Pydantic parsing.
E   Divergence detected: Trajectory replay cannot advance to state ACB_15.
=========================== 1 failed in 0.04s ==================================
```

The regression trace above illustrates a practical failure mode uncovered during offline trace replay. A refactored supervisor parser enforced strict Pydantic validation on unified diff strings, breaking backward compatibility with an unescaped markdown format that the historical agent had successfully handled via a legacy regex fallback.

Because the test ran against an archived event log, the failure was identified in $40\text{ ms}$ on local CPU infrastructure, pin-pointing the exact turn ($t=14$) and token payload where the supervisor logic diverged. By decoupling supervisor validation from live model inference, trace-driven regression harnesses provide deterministic guarantees that platform changes preserve operational behavior across real-world workloads.

Trajectory reconstruction succeeds only as long as the supervisor's state transition function $\delta$ can faithfully interpret historical event streams. However, when the runtime attempts to execute live trajectories or verify deterministic behavior across different hardware nodes, subtle sources of non-determinism—floating-point reduction order in GPU kernels, dynamic wall-clock system calls, and unseeded pseudorandom number generators—threaten replay fidelity. What systems techniques isolate and eliminate these entropy sources to guarantee bit-exact execution?

## Replay Divergence Diagnostics {#sec-vol3-persistence-non-determinism}

An autonomous software-engineering agent executing a multi-file refactoring task halts unexpectedly at turn $t=42$ due to an unhandled supervisor timeout. To diagnose the fault, an engineer retrieves the exact model weights, fixes the sampling temperature to $T=0$, restores the target repository to the identical Git commit hash, and launches an offline reproduction run on a secondary GPU cluster. Instead of reproducing the timeout at turn $t=42$, the trajectory abruptly diverges at turn $t=6$: the model selects an entirely different tool call, emits an unescaped shell argument, triggers an early syntax error, and terminates without ever reaching the target failure state. The bug cannot be reproduced, the crash dump is useless, and post-mortem analysis grinds to a halt.

**Bit-exact trajectory replay is disrupted by non-deterministic sampling, floating-point kernel race conditions, and dynamic wall-clocks; runtimes must virtualize and record all entropy sources.** A foundation model cannot be treated as a deterministic mathematical function $f(\mathbf{x}) \to \mathbf{y}$ across distinct hardware nodes, kernel versions, or execution passes. In an agentic system, minute non-determinisms at the micro-architectural or operating system layer do not remain localized perturbations; because autoregressive decoding feeds generated tokens directly back into subsequent attention contexts, a single flipped bit or altered token at turn $t$ propagates exponentially across subsequent turns. Constructing a dependable diagnostic and recovery engine requires systematically identifying every physical source of trajectory entropy, establishing virtualization boundaries to capture ambient nondeterminism, and enforcing observation escrow during replay.

### Taxonomy of Trajectory Entropy Sources

Entropy enters an agentic execution loop through four distinct architectural strata: stochastic inference parameters, GPU micro-architectural scheduling, dynamic host operating system interfaces, and mutable external environments. Operating systems engineers traditionally classify non-determinism into internal software state and external asynchronous I/O; in agentic runtimes, this boundary shifts because the core computational engine—the parallel matrix execution pipeline on hardware accelerators—is itself a major source of internal non-determinism.

The first and most obvious source of non-determinism is stochastic temperature sampling. When an inference runtime evaluates next-token predictions with a temperature parameter $T > 0$, the decode loop draws tokens randomly from the resulting categorical distribution. Unless the pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) state and seed are explicitly pinned and preserved, consecutive forward passes over identical prompt prefixes yield different token sequences. While pinning the PRNG seed provides statistical repeatability on a single isolated thread, it remains insufficient to guarantee bit-exact execution on modern parallel inference servers.

::: {.column-margin}
**Floating-Point Non-Associativity**
Under IEEE 754 arithmetic, addition is not associative: $(a \oplus b) \oplus c \neq a \oplus (b \oplus c)$. In parallel reduction kernels, changing the arrival order of partial sums changes the round-off error in the final floating-point significand.
:::

The second and more pernicious source of entropy arises from floating-point non-associativity in parallel GPU reduction kernels. High-performance matrix multiplication (GEMM) and fused multi-head attention kernels execute parallel reductions across thousands of streaming multiprocessor (SM) threads. As formalized by David Goldberg (1991), floating-point addition under IEEE 754 standards does not satisfy mathematical associativity. In parallel reduction trees where thread warps schedule dynamically based on DRAM bank contention, cache hits, and clock throttling, the exact summation order of partial products varies from run to run. Consequently, even when evaluating an identical prompt prefix at greedy decoding ($T=0$), the raw logit values for vocabulary tokens can drift by small floating-point epsilons ($\sim 10^{-6}$ to $10^{-4}$). If the two highest-ranking candidate tokens have logit margins smaller than this micro-architectural drift, the greedy `argmax` operator flips. A single flipped token alters the key-value context for all subsequent decode steps, leading to complete trajectory divergence within a handful of generated words.

```
       Host OS Stratum           System Calls (gettimeofday, getpid, urandom)
             │                   ├── Leak dynamic timestamps into prompts
             ▼                   └── Create non-reproducible UUID identifiers
  ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ Agent Supervisor Loop │◄───── External Environment Mutex
  └──────────┬────────────┘      └── Tool observation changes across replay
             │
             ▼                   Floating-Point Kernel Scheduling
     [Inference Engine]          ├── Warp arrival race conditions in GEMM
             │                   └── Asynchronous atomicAdd logit drift
             ▼
     [Token Emission] ──────────► Greedy Argmax Flip at t_diverge
```

The third stratum involves dynamic host operating system state leaked into prompts and control structures. Agent supervisors frequently inject metadata into system prompts, tool schemas, or scratchpads: current wall-clock timestamps via `time.time()`, host process identifiers via `getpid()`, local file paths, or random correlation identifiers via `uuid.uuid4()`. When a supervisor passes dynamic timestamps into an LLM context, the model conditions its reasoning on values that can never naturally repeat during subsequent execution. Furthermore, file system iterators that traverse directory trees without explicit collation return directory entries in raw inode order, which varies across file systems, container instances, and operating system kernels.

The fourth stratum encompasses external environment mutation. An agent does not operate in a hermetic computational vacuum; its primary purpose is interacting with external tools, HTTP endpoints, databases, and operating system shells. Between a production failure at time $t_{\text{live}}$ and a diagnostic replay session at time $t_{\text{replay}}$, external REST APIs change their response payloads, public search engines update their indices, remote Git repositories accept new commits, and local filesystems reflect intermediate mutations. If the replay harness allows the agent to execute real tool invocations against live external services, the observations returned to the agent will differ from historical execution, instantly invalidating the state trajectory.

| Entropy Stratum | Physical Mechanism | Impact on Trajectory | Runtime Isolation & Mitigation Strategy |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Stochastic Decoding** | Multinomial token selection with $T > 0$. | Completely divergent token outputs from identical prefix. | Explicit PRNG seed recording; log probability capture; token-level event replay. |
| **GPU Micro-Architecture** | Warp scheduling races during parallel reductions in GEMM/attention. | Sub-epsilon logit drift flipping greedy `argmax` selection. | Deterministic reduction algorithms; fixed accumulation ordering; token-stream escrow. |
| **Host System State** | Dynamic syscalls (`gettimeofday`, `getpid`, `getrandom`, `readdir`). | Unrepeatable timestamps and identifiers embedded in prompt context. | System call virtualization; PRNG sequence virtualization; strict canonical collation. |
| **External Environment** | Modifying external filesystems, databases, and third-party APIs. | Observation drift yielding divergent planning decisions. | Observation mocking; Write-Ahead Log (WAL) escrow; sandbox snapshot rollbacks. |
: Non-determinism classification matrix and runtime mitigation strategies. {#tbl-vol3-nondeterminism-mitigation}

### Floating-Point Non-Associativity and Logit Flips

To understand why bit-exact reproduction fails on identical GPU clusters under greedy decoding ($T=0$), one must inspect the arithmetic pipeline of parallel tensor reduction. During the prefill and decode stages of autoregressive inference, computing the attention score matrix $\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^T / \sqrt{d_k}$ and aggregating value vectors $\mathbf{O} = \text{Softmax}(\mathbf{S})\mathbf{V}$ requires summing millions of floating-point products across parallel SIMD lanes.

Modern accelerator architectures optimize throughput by utilizing atomic floating-point accumulation instructions (such as `atomicAdd` in CUDA) or dynamic reduction trees across thread blocks. In an accelerator with hundreds of streaming multiprocessors, the physical completion order of thread blocks depends on dynamic runtime conditions: memory bus congestion, L2 cache bank collisions, temperature-induced frequency scaling, and thread block dispatch scheduling. Because floating-point representations allocate a fixed number of bits to the significand (10 bits for IEEE 754 half-precision FP16; 7 bits for Brain Floating Point BF16), round-off occurs at every pairwise addition.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example: Logit Flip via Non-Associative Attention Reduction"}
Consider an inference pass for a model with vocabulary size $V = 128{,}000$, hidden dimension $d = 4096$, and sequence length $L = 2048$, evaluating the final linear projection layer $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{h} \mathbf{W}_{\text{vocab}}$ under BF16 precision. Suppose that for two candidate tokens—Token A (representing identifier `"write"`) and Token B (representing identifier `"save"`)—the exact mathematical dot products before rounding are:

$$\mathbf{z}_{\text{ideal}}[A] = 14.20012, \quad \mathbf{z}_{\text{ideal}}[B] = 14.20008$$

The margin separating the two candidates is $\Delta = \mathbf{z}_{\text{ideal}}[A] - \mathbf{z}_{\text{ideal}}[B] = 0.00004 = 4 \times 10^{-5}$.

The projection computes $\mathbf{z}[i] = \sum_{k=1}^{d} \mathbf{h}[k] \mathbf{W}_{\text{vocab}}[k, i]$ using parallel reduction across $P = 128$ threads per warp. In BF16, the machine epsilon is $\epsilon_{\text{mach}} = 2^{-7} \approx 7.81 \times 10^{-3}$. In a tree reduction where summation order is strictly fixed, round-off error accumulates deterministically. However, in an unconstrained atomic accumulation pipeline, partial sums arrive out of order.

Suppose Run 1 schedules warps such that smaller partial sums accumulate first, yielding a net rounding perturbation of $\delta_1 = -2 \times 10^{-5}$ on Token A and $+3 \times 10^{-5}$ on Token B:

$$\mathbf{z}_{\text{Run 1}}[A] = 14.20010, \quad \mathbf{z}_{\text{Run 1}}[B] = 14.20011 \implies \text{Argmax selects Token B (`\"save\"`)}$$

In Run 2, memory bank conflicts delay thread block 3, altering the accumulation order such that $\delta_2 = +2 \times 10^{-5}$ on Token A and $-1 \times 10^{-5}$ on Token B:

$$\mathbf{z}_{\text{Run 2}}[A] = 14.20014, \quad \mathbf{z}_{\text{Run 2}}[B] = 14.20007 \implies \text{Argmax selects Token A (`\"write\"`)}$$

The logit ranking inverts purely due to micro-architectural scheduling jitter. If Token A corresponds to a structured tool call delimiter while Token B triggers standard prose generation, the supervisor's state transition function $\delta$ branches into an entirely disconnected control state.
:::

Systems engineers have attempted to enforce determinism at the GPU kernel layer by replacing asynchronous atomic additions with deterministic segmented scan algorithms or fixed-order reduction trees. While deterministic GEMM implementations exist (such as setting `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8` in CUDA environments), they introduce measurable performance penalties. Enforcing deterministic reductions restricts warp scheduling freedom, prevents opportunistic memory coalescing, and disables dynamic load balancing across SMs, imposing a 10% to 25% throughput reduction on dense model serving.

More fundamentally, deterministic CUDA flags only guarantee repeatability across runs conducted on the *identical physical hardware model with the identical compute capability, microcode version, and SM count*. A trajectory generated on an NVIDIA H100 (132 SMs, FP8/BF16 Tensor Cores) cannot be deterministically reproduced at the kernel level on an A100 (108 SMs) or an L40S, because the thread block tiling dimensions and warp partition topologies differ fundamentally. Consequently, relying on GPU-level arithmetic determinism for trajectory replay is an architectural dead end for portable systems.

### Virtualizing Time, Entropy, and Observation Escrow

Because bit-level model determinism cannot be achieved portably across hardware tiers, a resilient agent runtime must apply the classical systems principle of virtualization. Rather than attempting to force the underlying execution hardware to behave deterministically, the supervisor interposes on the boundary between the agent and all ambient entropy sources. This design separates execution into two operating modes: *recording mode* during live execution, and *virtualized replay mode* during diagnostic analysis.

::: {.column-margin}
**Crash-Only Verification**
Following George Candea et al. (2004), systems should treat recovery paths as first-class operational paths. Virtualized replay ensures that post-crash state reconstruction relies on immutable, recorded event streams rather than live environment synchronization.
:::

Virtualizing host entropy requires trapping every nondeterministic system call before its return value can enter the model context or supervisor state machine. When an agent process initializes, the runtime injects an interception shim (via an `LD_PRELOAD` shared library, an eBPF tracepoint probe, or a custom execution runtime sandbox). This shim intercepts four critical system interfaces:

1. **Wall-Clock Virtualization:** Calls to `clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME)`, `gettimeofday()`, or language-level wrappers (`time.time()`) are intercepted. In recording mode, the real system time is returned and simultaneously written to the event stream as a side-effect event $e_{\text{clock}}$. In replay mode, the interceptor blocks access to the hardware clock and returns the recorded sequence of timestamps from the event log, ensuring monotonic and identical time progression.
2. **Pseudorandom Number Generators:** Calls to `/dev/urandom`, `getrandom()`, or framework-level seeds (`random.seed()`, `torch.manual_seed()`) are intercepted. The initial seed and all consumed random sequences are logged. During replay, the pseudo-random stream is regenerated deterministically from the recorded seed.
3. **Identifier Generation:** Dynamic generation of UUIDs, process identifiers (`getpid()`), and socket descriptors is trapped. The runtime replaces random UUID generation with a deterministic counter hashed with the trajectory's base execution ID: $\text{UUID}_k = \text{HMAC-SHA256}(\text{TrajectoryID}, k)$.
4. **Filesystem Traversal Collation:** Calls to `getdents64` or `readdir()` are intercepted to enforce strict lexicographical sorting on returned directory entries, neutralizing kernel-dependent inode ordering.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     RECORDING MODE                          |
|                                                             |
|  Agent Supervisor ──► Syscall Shim ──► Host OS Kernel       |
|                            │                                |
|                            ▼                                |
|                   Append to Event Log                       |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                      REPLAY MODE                            |
|                                                             |
|  Agent Supervisor ──► Syscall Shim ──X (Kernel Trapped)     |
|                            ▲                                |
|                            │                                |
|                   Inject from Event Log                     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

While host virtualization eliminates environment entropy within the supervisor process, it does not resolve divergence within external tools. When an agent invokes an external action $a_{\text{ext}}$ (such as querying an API, executing a database transaction, or running a build script), repeating this invocation during replay risks secondary non-determinism or unintended external mutation.

To neutralize external tool divergence, the runtime implements *observation escrow*. In recording mode, whenever an external action $a_{\text{ext}}$ executes, its complete observation payload $e_{\text{obs}}$—including standard output, standard error, exit codes, HTTP headers, and response bodies—is flushed to the append-only Write-Ahead Log before being returned to the model. In replay mode, the runtime completely disconnects the external RPC transport. When the supervisor's state machine reaches the dispatch phase for $a_{\text{ext}}$, the action is intercepted by an observation mocking engine. The mock engine validates that the proposed action matches the recorded action schema; if valid, it injects the historical observation $e_{\text{obs}}$ directly from the event log without dispatching network packets or modifying external filesystems.

```python
# Trace-level verification diff demonstrating logit-induced replay divergence
--- recorded_trajectory_step_14.json
+++ replayed_trajectory_step_14.json
@@ -6,9 +6,9 @@
   "entropy_sources": {
-    "wall_clock_ms": 1729340112405,
-    "host_pid": 84120
+    "wall_clock_ms": 1729340119881,  # UNVIRTUALIZED SYSCALL DETECTED
+    "host_pid": 84993
   },
   "proposed_action": {
-    "tool": "file_search", "pattern": "*.py", "order": "lexicographical"
+    "tool": "file_search", "pattern": "*.py", "order": "inode"
   }
```

The realization that bit-exact model re-execution is computationally expensive and fragile across heterogeneous hardware leads to an essential architectural decoupling: **Trajectory Verification vs. Model Re-Execution**.

When diagnosing supervisor state machines, distributed consensus, or tool orchestration failures, the runtime does not re-invoke the foundation model at all. Instead, it performs *trace-driven verification*: the recorded tokens and tool proposals are replayed directly from the immutable event ledger into the supervisor logic, verifying that the supervisor's state transition function $\delta(\mathbf{S}_t, e_t) = \mathbf{S}_{t+1}$ faithfully reproduces the expected intermediate states.

If an engineer specifically needs to evaluate model divergence across new model weights, quantization schemes, or inference engines, the system runs *divergence analysis mode*. Here, the model is re-invoked on the historical prompt prefixes, and the runtime computes token-level log-probability divergence (Kullback-Leibler divergence over logits):

$$D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{live}} \parallel P_{\text{replay}}) = \sum_{w \in \mathcal{V}} P_{\text{live}}(w) \log \left( \frac{P_{\text{live}}(w)}{P_{\text{replay}}(w)} \right)$$

By establishing strict virtualization boundaries around wall-clocks, trapping PRNG entropy, escrowing external tool observations, and measuring logit-level divergence, the runtime guarantees that diagnostic analysis operates with mathematical precision. An engineer can bisect a failing trajectory, inspect intermediate supervisor state transitions, and verify algorithmic invariants without being misled by floating-point hardware races or drifting external APIs.

Sealing ambient entropy channels transforms an executing trajectory into a closed, self-contained computational state defined entirely by its serialized Agent Control Block ($\text{ACB}_t$), its append-only event stream $\mathcal{E}$, and its isolated sandbox state overlays. Because the runtime no longer depends on static physical host bindings, local hardware clocks, or unrepeatable GPU reduction schedules, an active trajectory becomes fully portable across space and time. If a worker node experiences physical hardware failure, thermal throttling, or spot-instance preemption, the supervisor can detach this serialized state package and reconstruct the running task on a completely different physical machine without loss of execution integrity. How does a distributed runtime coordinate the live migration of an active trajectory across physical cluster nodes without dropping inflight RPCs or duplicating external side effects?

## Live Trajectory Migration {#sec-vol3-persistence-migration}

Physical worker nodes in modern cloud datacenters are fundamentally ephemeral. Hardware components suffer unrecoverable bit flips, thermal throttling forces hypervisors to throttle clock frequencies, and hyperscale cloud providers dynamically reclaim spot and preemptible compute instances to balance multi-tenant capacity. When an agentic workload executes an extended software refactoring task spanning forty reasoning turns, dozens of test-suite runs, and hundreds of intermediate file modifications, binding the execution lifecycle to the volatile memory and local storage of a single physical machine creates an intolerable operational vulnerability. Terminating a three-hour software migration task because an underlying host received a 30-second eviction notice wastes millions of input tokens, inflates operational costs, and risks leaving external systems in an inconsistent state.

**Decoupling an active trajectory's execution state into a serialized supervisory control block, an append-only event stream, and a copy-on-write filesystem overlay allows the runtime to evacuate and resume a running agent across physical worker nodes without task loss or duplicate side effects.** Rather than treating an autonomous agent as an opaque operating system process tied to specific CPU registers and virtual memory page tables, the runtime treats the trajectory as an explicitly factored distributed state machine. By synchronizing this factored state at clean conversational turn boundaries, the supervisor transforms an unexpected hardware eviction from a catastrophic crash into a routine, sub-second live migration.

### The Preemption Imperative and Evacuation Windows

In hyperscale infrastructure, transient compute instances—offered as AWS Spot Instances, Google Cloud Spot VMs, or Azure Spot Virtual Machines—provide between 70% and 90% cost discounts relative to on-demand pricing. For enterprise agent fleets running thousands of long-horizon software engineering, code synthesis, or data pipeline trajectories continuously, operating exclusively on on-demand instances imposes prohibitive capital expenditure. However, these steep cost savings come with a strict systems trade-off: instances are subject to involuntary reclamation whenever higher-priority on-demand demand spikes.

::: {.column-margin}
Historically, process and virtual machine migration sought to preserve volatile memory bit-by-bit across physical hosts. Clark et al. [-@clark2005live] pioneered iterative pre-copy memory migration for whole virtual machines, while Nelson et al. [-@nelson2005fast] solved network interface and swap re-mapping. In agentic systems, because the underlying neural weights reside remotely in an inference cluster and the agent's logic is mediated by an unprivileged supervisor, we do not migrate gigabytes of raw process RAM; we migrate the structured semantic state.
:::

Cloud providers notify virtual machines of impending preemption via hypervisor interrupts, metadata ACPI signals, or polling endpoints. As summarized in @tbl-vol3-preemption-deadlines, the evacuation window $\Delta t_{\text{evac}}$ granted to the host ranges from two minutes down to a meager fifteen seconds. If the runtime fails to persist dirty state and relinquish network leases before $\Delta t_{\text{evac}}$ elapses, the hypervisor abruptly issues a hard reset (`SIGKILL` equivalent), destroying all uncommitted memory and ephemeral NVMe storage.

| Cloud Provider & Instance Tier | Evacuation Warning Mechanism | Warning Window ($\Delta t_{\text{evac}}$) | Hardware State Reclaimed |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **AWS EC2 Spot Instances** | Instance Action Metadata / CloudWatch Event | 120 seconds | Host RAM, Ephemeral NVMe, Local Network Interface |
| **Google Cloud Spot VMs** | ACPI G2 Soft-Off / Metadata Query | 30 seconds | Host RAM, Ephemeral Local SSD, Private IP Lease |
| **Azure Spot VMs** | Scheduled Events REST API | 30 seconds | Host RAM, Ephemeral Temp Disk, Hypervisor VCPU |
| **Equinix Metal Bare Metal** | Out-of-Band IPMI Alert | 15 seconds | Motherboard RAM, Physical SATA/NVMe, Hardware MAC |

: Industry standard preemption and evacuation warning windows for transient compute. {#tbl-vol3-preemption-deadlines}

The systems challenge is fundamentally quantitative. Let $S_{\text{total}}$ represent the aggregate volume of dirty state generated by the trajectory that is not yet durable on remote persistent storage, and let $B_{\text{net}}$ represent the available outbound network bandwidth from the evicted host to shared durable storage or the target peer node. Evacuation is physically feasible if and only if the sum of the serialization latency $t_{\text{ser}}$, the network transfer time $t_{\text{xfer}}$, and the remote registration handshake $t_{\text{ack}}$ strictly satisfies the deadline:

$$\Delta t_{\text{evac}} > t_{\text{ser}} + t_{\text{xfer}} + t_{\text{ack}} = t_{\text{ser}} + \frac{S_{\text{total}}}{B_{\text{net}}} + t_{\text{ack}}$$ {#eq-vol3-evacuation-deadline}

If an agent runtime attempts a naive migration by dumping an uncompressed 16 GiB container root filesystem and its entire supervisory process heap over a congested 1 Gbps ($125\text{ MB/s}$) top-of-rack network link, transfer time alone requires $137.4\text{ seconds}$, guaranteed to violate the 30-second Google Cloud deadline. To guarantee migration feasibility, the runtime must drastically minimize $S_{\text{total}}$ through strict state factorizing.

### Clean Turn-Boundary Quiescence

A running agent cannot be safely serialized at an arbitrary, uncoordinated microsecond. Autoregressive foundation models execute token-by-token generation across remote inference servers; tool calls execute asynchronous remote procedure calls (RPCs) against external compilers, databases, and third-party APIs; and local execution environments execute multi-threaded bash subprocesses inside isolated Linux namespaces. Initiating state capture while an asynchronous HTTP tool mutation is in-flight creates an undefined distributed state: the destination host cannot discern whether the remote endpoint received the payload, executed the mutation, or failed silently.

To prevent partial mutations and dangling side effects, the supervisor enforces *clean turn-boundary quiescence*. The execution lifecycle of an autonomous agent naturally alternates between two distinct phases:

1. **The In-Flight Mutation Phase:** The runtime is either streaming autoregressive tokens from the neural engine or actively awaiting response bytes from an external tool execution inside the sandbox.
2. **The Turn Quiescence Boundary:** The runtime has parsed the complete tool observation $e_{\text{obs}}$, verified schema conformity, appended the event to the Write-Ahead Log (WAL), updated the Agent Control Block ($\text{ACB}_t$), and has not yet submitted the subsequent prefill request to the model inference engine.

```
       Source Worker Node                        Destination Worker Node
  +--------------------------+                 +--------------------------+
  |  Agent Control Block     |                 |                          |
  |  [ ACB_t (State Machine) |                 |                          |
  +-------------+------------+                 |                          |
                |                              |                          |
     (1) Drain / Quiesce                       |                          |
                |                              |                          |
  +-------------v------------+                 |                          |
  | Ephemeral Sandbox FS     |                 |                          |
  | [ OverlayFS upperdir ]   |                 |                          |
  +-------------+------------+                 |                          |
                |                              |                          |
    (2) Sync Delta Blocks                      |                          |
                |                              |                          |
                v                              |                          |
     +--------------------+                    |                          |
     | Shared Persistent  |                    |                          |
     | Storage Fabric     |                    |                          |
     | (NVMe-oF / S3)     |                    |                          |
     +----------+---------+                    |                          |
                |                              |                          |
                |  (3) Re-bind & Mount         |                          |
                +----------------------------->+                          |
                                               |  +--------------------+  |
                                               |  | Restored Sandbox   |  |
                                               |  | [ Re-hydrated ACB ]|  |
                                               |  +--------------------+  |
                                               +--------------------------+
```
![Live trajectory migration sequence across source worker, shared storage fabric, and destination worker.](images/svg/fig-vol3-trajectory-migration.svg){#fig-vol3-trajectory-migration width="100%"}

When the host operating system catches an impending eviction signal (e.g., via a POSIX signal handler trapping `SIGTERM` or a background daemon polling the hypervisor metadata socket), it transitions the trajectory's local supervisor into an `EVACUATION_PENDING` state.

If the agent is currently awaiting an external tool invocation, the supervisor allows the socket to drain until a strict per-tool timeout $\tau_{\text{tool}}$ expires. If the tool completes within $\tau_{\text{tool}}$, the resulting $e_{\text{obs}}$ is written to the local log buffer, flushed to durable storage via `fsync()`, and the agent transitions to the quiescence boundary. If the tool fails to return within $\tau_{\text{tool}}$, the supervisor forcefully terminates the tool handle, records an artificial `e_{\text{abort}}` event marking the RPC as aborted due to preemption, and rolls back any uncommitted speculative local state.

Once the turn boundary is established, all CPU scheduling within the local sandbox container is frozen via Linux control groups (`cgroups v2` freezer subsystem). Freezing the cgroup guarantees that no hidden background threads, pending disk writes, or timers modify the filesystem or memory during the subsequent serialization protocol.

### The Tripartite State Migration Protocol

Because an agentic system separates reasoning (delegated to a stateless inference engine) from execution and memory (governed by the local supervisor), its total dynamic state factors cleanly into three independent layers. As detailed in @tbl-vol3-tripartite-migration, each layer possesses distinct size characteristics, synchronization mechanisms, and durability requirements.

| State Layer | Component Constituents | Typical Size | Persistence Mechanism | Target Recovery Time |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Control Plane ($\text{ACB}_t$)** | Finite state machine registers, token consumption metrics, active tool capability leases, pseudo-random generator seeds, context window offsets. | $10\text{ KiB} - 500\text{ KiB}$ | Structured Protocol Buffer serialized directly to WAL header. | $< 5\text{ ms}$ |
| **Causal Log ($\mathcal{E}$)** | Ordered sequence of validated events $e_0, \dots, e_t$, cryptographic hashes, policy authorizations, token usage proofs. | $1\text{ MiB} - 50\text{ MiB}$ | Append-only log segment flushed to shared distributed storage via synchronous TLS stream. | $< 100\text{ ms}$ |
| **Sandbox Environment ($\mathbf{S}_t$)** | Modified source files, git working trees, intermediate build artifacts, temporary debug outputs located in OverlayFS `upperdir`. | $10\text{ MiB} - 2\text{ GiB}$ | Block-level delta replication over NVMe-oF or asynchronous compressed `rsync` archive. | $500\text{ ms} - 10\text{ s}$ |

: The tripartite state migration decomposition model. Separating control, causal history, and environment layers bounds downtime. {#tbl-vol3-tripartite-migration}

#### 1. ACB State Serialization

The Agent Control Block ($\text{ACB}_t$) represents the authoritative control state of the supervisor at turn $t$. Unlike an operating system process control block, which must capture volatile machine registers, translation lookaside buffer (TLB) state, and memory segment descriptors, the $\text{ACB}_t$ contains purely semantic runtime metadata.

During the serialization step, the supervisor packs:
- The discrete state machine state (e.g., `AWAITING_MODEL_INFERENCE`, `VALIDATING_TOOL_INPUT`).
- Cumulative token accounting records (input, output, and cache-hit token tallies).
- Active capability leases, including scoped subagent authorization tokens, unexpired cryptographic API keys, and temporary sandboxed network credentials granted under Zero Ambient Authority ($A=0$).
- Deterministic pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) state sequences, ensuring that any downstream stochastic sampling algorithms can reproduce their internal paths if required.
- The high-water mark sequence ID of the event stream $\mathcal{E}$.

Because the $\text{ACB}_t$ is structured as a compact Protocol Buffer schema without raw memory pointers, serialization consumes less than five milliseconds and yields a payload rarely exceeding a few hundred kilobytes.

#### 2. Filesystem Delta Synchronization

The most substantial component of an agent's physical footprint is its sandbox execution environment. Agents specialized for software engineering edit source files, compile binaries, install language runtime dependencies via package managers, and generate test logs. Preserving this environment without transferring tens of gigabytes of base OS dependencies requires a union filesystem architecture, typically implemented via the Linux kernel's `OverlayFS`.

In an OverlayFS deployment, the sandbox filesystem consists of three directories:
- A read-only `lowerdir` containing the base container image (Ubuntu OS, Python runtimes, standard compilers, tool binaries). This layer is completely immutable and pre-cached locally across all worker nodes in the compute cluster.
- A writable `upperdir` hosted on an ephemeral local filesystem. Every file edit, newly created source file, or deleted directory performed by the agent is recorded exclusively as a copy-on-write delta inside `upperdir`.
- A `workdir` utilized by the kernel for atomic directory operations.

```
       Source Node                                Destination Node
+-------------------------+                   +-------------------------+
| Writable upperdir       | -- Sync Delta --> | Restored upperdir       |
| (142 MiB Agent Edits)   |    (Network)      | (142 MiB Agent Edits)   |
+-------------------------+                   +-------------------------+
| Immutable lowerdir      |                   | Immutable lowerdir      |
| (12 GiB Base Image)     |                   | (12 GiB Pre-cached)     |
+-------------------------+                   +-------------------------+
```

Because the `lowerdir` is already present on the destination worker node, the migration runtime completely ignores the base image. It needs only to synchronize the modified bytes residing in `upperdir`.

To maximize efficiency under tight preemption deadlines, the runtime employs an *iterative pre-copy* strategy directly inspired by hypervisor memory migration algorithms:

1. **Continuous Background Sync:** While the agent is actively executing, a low-priority background daemon periodically mirrors newly modified blocks in `upperdir` to network-attached block storage (such as an NVMe-over-Fabrics target or distributed object volume) using differential file block hashing.
2. **Final Quiescent Delta:** At the moment of turn-boundary quiescence, the filesystem cgroup is frozen, and an explicit `syncfs()` syscall flushes the OS dirty page cache to disk. The migration agent sweeps the `upperdir` for blocks dirtied since the last background pass, tars the differential stream, applies lightweight LZ4 compression, and dispatches the final delta across the network link.

#### 3. Tool Channel and IPC Re-binding

The final phase of the tripartite protocol reconciles external communication channels. While an agent's memory and disk can be serialized, active operating system communication channels—such as TCP sockets, UNIX domain sockets connected to local sandbox bridges, and inter-process communication (IPC) pipes to subagents—cannot be directly transplanted across physical network interfaces.

The supervisor addresses this by enforcing *declarative channel virtualization*. The agent's application code never communicates directly with raw host file descriptors. Instead, all input and output flows through a mediated RPC gateway. During the migration freeze:

1. **Channel Revocation:** The source supervisor sends a `MIGRATION_DETACH` control packet over its internal UNIX sockets to the sandbox container, terminates all local proxy tunnels, and invalidates temporary mutual TLS (mTLS) session tokens.
2. **Lease Transfer:** The source supervisor contacts the centralized lease coordinator, relinquishing its node-specific execution lease while atomically claiming a handoff token bound to the destination worker's network identity.
3. **Channel Re-binding:** Upon booting the restored container on the destination host, the new supervisor provisions a fresh set of local UNIX domain sockets, establishes authenticated mTLS sessions with external tool endpoints, updates internal routing tables for any attached child subagents, and re-attaches the virtual standard input and output streams.

From the perspective of the external tool service, the migration appears simply as a momentary network keep-alive pause followed by an authenticated session resumption.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example: Calculating Migration Budgets Under Hard Preemption Deadlines"}
Consider an autonomous coding agent executing on a Google Cloud Spot VM that receives an ACPI preemption warning providing an evacuation window of $\Delta t_{\text{evac}} = 30\text{ seconds}$.

The agent operates with the following physical footprint:
- An Agent Control Block ($\text{ACB}_t$) of size $S_{\text{ACB}} = 128\text{ KiB}$.
- An unflushed local event log tail of size $S_{\text{WAL}} = 4.5\text{ MiB}$.
- An OverlayFS `upperdir` containing dirty source edits, a compiled Rust binary, and test artifacts totaling $S_{\text{upper}} = 280\text{ MiB}$.
- The base container image is $14\text{ GiB}$ (pre-cached on the destination node).

The host is connected to an enterprise datacenter network fabric offering an effective outbound bandwidth of $B_{\text{net}} = 1\text{ Gbps}$ ($125\text{ MB/s}$), operating at an average network utilization of 20% background load (yielding $B_{\text{avail}} = 100\text{ MB/s}$). The local NVMe disk subsystem reads at $1.5\text{ GB/s}$. LZ4 compression achieves an average compression ratio of $r = 2.1:1$ on the compilation and source artifacts, operating at a compression throughput of $C_{\text{rate}} = 400\text{ MB/s}$.

Let us calculate the total migration latency $T_{\text{migration}}$ and determine whether the evacuation succeeds within the 30-second budget:

**Step 1: Quiescence and Drainage Latency ($t_{\text{quiesce}}$)**
The agent is currently awaiting an in-flight compiler check. The tool completes within $t_{\text{tool}} = 1.8\text{ seconds}$. The cgroup freezer suspends all container processes in $t_{\text{freeze}} = 15\text{ ms}$.
$$t_{\text{quiesce}} = 1.8\text{ s} + 0.015\text{ s} = 1.815\text{ seconds}$$

**Step 2: Serialization and Compression Latency ($t_{\text{ser}}$)**
Serializing the $\text{ACB}_t$ takes $3\text{ ms}$. Flushing the WAL requires an `fsync()` taking $8\text{ ms}$.
Compressing the $280\text{ MiB}$ `upperdir` delta:
$$t_{\text{comp}} = \frac{280\text{ MiB}}{400\text{ MB/s}} = 0.70\text{ seconds}$$
Compressed size of the filesystem delta:
$$S_{\text{comp}} = \frac{280\text{ MiB}}{2.1} \approx 133.33\text{ MiB}$$
Total payload to transmit across the network fabric:
$$S_{\text{total}} = S_{\text{ACB}} + S_{\text{WAL}} + S_{\text{comp}} = 0.125\text{ MiB} + 4.5\text{ MiB} + 133.33\text{ MiB} = 137.96\text{ MiB}$$

**Step 3: Network Transfer Latency ($t_{\text{xfer}}$)**
Transmitting the compressed payload over the available network bandwidth:
$$t_{\text{xfer}} = \frac{137.96\text{ MiB}}{100\text{ MB/s}} = 1.38\text{ seconds}$$

**Step 4: Destination Restoration and Re-binding ($t_{\text{restore}}$)**
On the destination worker node:
- Container initialization and mounting the pre-cached `lowerdir` with the unpacked `upperdir`: $t_{\text{mount}} = 0.45\text{ seconds}$.
- Decompressing the $133.33\text{ MiB}$ delta at $1.2\text{ GB/s}$: $t_{\text{decomp}} = 0.11\text{ seconds}$.
- Deserializing the $\text{ACB}_t$, replaying the trailing $4.5\text{ MiB}$ WAL events, and acquiring new tool socket leases: $t_{\text{rebind}} = 0.12\text{ seconds}$.
$$t_{\text{restore}} = 0.45\text{ s} + 0.11\text{ s} + 0.12\text{ s} = 0.68\text{ seconds}$$

**Step 5: Total Migration Latency Evaluation**
Summing the distinct phases:
$$T_{\text{migration}} = t_{\text{quiesce}} + t_{\text{ser}} + t_{\text{xfer}} + t_{\text{restore}} = 1.815 + 0.711 + 1.380 + 0.680 = 4.586\text{ seconds}$$

Because $T_{\text{migration}} = 4.59\text{ seconds} \ll \Delta t_{\text{evac}} = 30\text{ seconds}$, the tripartite migration completes comfortably within the preemption envelope, leaving a safety margin of more than 25 seconds before the cloud provider reclaims the hardware.
:::

### Failure Recovery and Fencing Tokens

What occurs if a network partition isolates the source node during migration, preventing the supervisor from confirming whether the destination node assumed control? In distributed systems, this hazard is known as the *split-brain anomaly*: two distinct supervisor processes on different physical machines believe they own the same trajectory, concurrently executing tool calls, emitting contradictory model queries, and corrupting external state.

To guarantee safety under network anomalies, live trajectory migration relies on *fencing tokens* coupled to a centralized consensus-backed lease manager. The lease coordinator maintains a monotonic generation counter $g \in \mathbb{N}$ associated with each active trajectory ID:

1. When the source node initiates evacuation, it attempts to atomically increment the generation counter from $g$ to $g+1$ and assign the new lease to the destination node.
2. If the source node becomes partitioned and fails to release its lease, the destination node waits for the source node's lease lease time-to-live ($T_{\text{lease}}$, typically 5 seconds) to expire. Once expired, the destination node forcefully acquires the lease with counter $g+1$.
3. Every external tool invocation, database mutation, and remote model inference request initiated by a supervisor must include its active generation token $g$.

If the partitioned source node attempts to issue a tool mutation with its stale token $g$, the mediated tool RPC gateway inspects the token, recognizes that generation $g+1$ has been registered, and summarily rejects the request with an authorization fault. The partitioned source node, recognizing its lease has been revoked, immediately executes a self-fencing crash (`abort()`), guaranteeing that only the newly migrated supervisor can advance the trajectory.

---

By cleanly separating supervisory control state, the append-only event stream, and ephemeral copy-on-write filesystem deltas, an agent runtime achieves robust physical portability. A long-horizon trajectory ceases to be a fragile, host-bound process; it becomes a resilient, relocatable computation that seamlessly hops across transient cloud infrastructure as physical conditions dictate.

However, as hundreds of concurrently migrating agents execute across enterprise clusters for weeks at a time, their append-only event logs expand monotonically. Every turn records large model prompts, verbose shell outputs, tool call JSON payloads, and diff patches. Left unmanaged, this accumulation exhausts high-throughput storage tiers and degrades historical replay performance. As thousands of autonomous agents generate gigabytes of event logs daily, how does the runtime manage storage costs without compromising compliance?

## Log Compaction Policies {#sec-vol3-persistence-compaction}

An uncompacted append-only event stream becomes an operational liability within hours of sustained agent execution. During a long-horizon coding or software maintenance task, an autonomous agent issuing repetitive build commands, unit tests, and repository searches accumulates vast quantities of unstructured stdout and stderr bytes. A single test failure trace or compiler error log can inject several megabytes of raw textual output into the event store, even though the model requires only the exit code and a handful of error lines to formulate its next repair hypothesis. Across thousands of concurrently running agents in an enterprise environment, unconstrained append-only logging exhausts the input/output operations per second (IOPS) and storage capacity of high-performance non-volatile storage, inflates snapshot restoration latency, and multiplies cloud archival costs.

**Trajectory storage must enforce multi-tier lifecycle compaction, pruning bulky ephemeral observation bytes while preserving the causal decision graph across Hot, Warm, and Cold storage tiers.**

Preserving durable records does not require retaining every ephemeral byte in perpetuity at maximum read availability. Just as classical database management systems distinguish between hot transactional write-ahead logs and cold historical backups, an agent runtime must treat trajectory persistence as a progressive data lifecycle. Storage systems for autonomous agents solve this challenge by decoupling the causal spine—the cryptographically verifiable sequence of model proposals, supervisor authorizations, and state transitions—from bulky, low-information observation payloads. By progressively demoting and compacting execution artifacts across distinct hardware storage tiers, runtimes maintain strict compliance and diagnostic auditability without letting storage costs scale linearly with raw tool output volume.

### Multi-Tier Storage Hierarchy: Hot, Warm, and Cold Planes

The storage requirements of an autonomous trajectory change radically across its lifecycle. While an agent is actively executing, the runtime prioritizes write latency and crash recovery throughput above all else. Every per-turn transition must be durably committed before the runtime triggers external side effects, demanding sub-millisecond append latency to prevent the supervisor from stalling the model's decode loop. Conversely, once an agent completes its assigned task, write frequency drops to zero, and the access pattern shifts from latency-sensitive sequential writes to ad-hoc query scans for debugging, regression testing, or regulatory audits.

```
       ▲                HOT TIER (< 24 Hours)
      / \        Active trajectories, local NVMe / RocksDB
     /   \       Sub-millisecond fsync(), uncompacted raw events
    /     \
   /       \            WARM TIER (1 - 30 Days)
  /         \    Completed trajectories, PostgreSQL / ClickHouse
 /           \   Metadata indexed, selective payload compaction
/             \
/───────────────\        COLD TIER (> 30 Days)
                 Immutable columnar archives, S3 / Parquet / Glacier
                 Cryptographic hashes retained, deep compliance storage
```

To balance these conflicting demands, modern agent platforms organize trajectory persistence into a three-tier hierarchy spanning Hot, Warm, and Cold physical storage planes, as illustrated in @fig-vol3-storage-pyramid.

![Multi-tier trajectory storage pyramid organizing event persistence across Hot, Warm, and Cold planes according to latency, compaction state, and lifecycle retention policies.](images/svg/fig-vol3-storage-pyramid.svg){#fig-vol3-storage-pyramid}

The *Hot Tier* serves active, running trajectories spanning the initial zero to twenty-four hour operational window. This tier is physically located on local non-volatile solid-state storage (NVMe SSDs) attached directly to the agent execution host, typically managed by an embedded Log-Structured Merge-tree (LSM-tree) engine such as RocksDB or an append-only raw file journal. The Hot Tier accepts synchronous Write-Ahead Log (WAL) flushes with explicit `fsync()` barriers on every operational turn. Because crash recovery requires restoring the exact, bit-for-bit control state of an interrupted agent, no compaction or data pruning is permitted in this plane; raw prompts, unedited tool observations, floating-point sampling parameters, and supervisor authorization records are stored in their entirety.

::: {.column-margin}
**Write Amplification in Tier Transitions**
Moving data from local LSM-trees to distributed columnar stores incurs write amplification. Runtimes mitigate this overhead by buffering completed turns in memory and streaming compacted batches directly to object storage via asynchronous background workers once a trajectory reaches a terminal state (`COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, or `ABORTED`).
:::

The *Warm Tier* houses completed or long-quiescent trajectories over a retention window of one to thirty days. Once an agent terminates or yields execution, its local journal is demoted to a centralized, distributed relational or analytical database cluster, such as PostgreSQL or ClickHouse. In this plane, the runtime strips away raw scratchpad buffers while indexing high-level metadata: trajectory identifiers, total token expenditures, wall-clock latencies, exit statuses, and tool invocation signatures. The Warm Tier empowers systems engineers to execute interactive SQL queries, run regression evaluations against known test suites, and isolate faulty reasoning trajectories without fetching multi-gigabyte disk images.

The *Cold Tier* provides long-term archival storage for trajectories older than thirty days, targeting regulatory compliance windows that often mandate data retention for three to seven years. In this plane, trajectories are serialized into immutable, highly compressed columnar formats, such as Apache Parquet files compressed with Zstandard, and uploaded to globally distributed object storage clusters (e.g., Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, or deep cold storage such as AWS Glacier). In the Cold Tier, storage density and read cost dominate system design; raw terminal streams are permanently discarded, leaving only structured event schemas, cryptographic execution digests, and audit certificates.

| Storage Dimension | Hot Tier (Execution) | Warm Tier (Triage & Eval) | Cold Tier (Compliance) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Physical Media** | Local Host NVMe SSD / DRAM | Distributed SSD Cluster | Distributed Object Storage / Tape |
| **Storage Engine** | Embedded LSM-Tree (RocksDB) | Relational / Columnar DB | Parquet on Object Store (S3) |
| **Target Latency** | $< 1\text{ ms}$ (Append) | $10\text{--}100\text{ ms}$ (Query) | $1\text{--}5\text{ s}$ (Batch Read) |
| **Payload State** | Raw, uncompacted bytes | Selectively pruned & digested | Columnar compressed, pruned |
| **Retention Horizon** | $0\text{ to }24\text{ hours}$ | $1\text{ to }30\text{ days}$ | $30\text{ days to }7\text{ years}$ |
| **Cost Profile** | Highest per GB; IOPS-bound | Moderate; query-optimized | Lowest per GB; capacity-bound |

: Architectural characteristics and hardware tradeoffs across trajectory persistence tiers. {#tbl-vol3-storage-tiers}

### Selective Payload Compaction and Epistemic Pruning

The core invariant of trajectory persistence states that any valid reconstruction must reproduce the supervisory control state $\text{ACB}_t$ without repeating historical external side effects. However, preserving the supervisory state does not require preserving every peripheral character produced by an external tool. When a compiler fails, the supervisor needs to know that the build failed and needs access to the relevant compiler diagnostic lines that the agent will parse to plan a correction. The thousands of intermediate lines indicating successful compilation of unaffected translation units provide zero epistemic value to future turns or post-incident audits.

Selective payload compaction exploits this asymmetry between causal relevance and raw textual volume. Rather than treating all event payloads as uniform binary blobs, the compaction engine classifies event data into two distinct operational classes: the *causal spine* and *ephemeral observations*.

```
UNCOMPACTED EVENT RECORD (Hot Tier):
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Turn: 42 | Event: TOOL_OBSERVATION | Tool: cargo_build                 │
│ Causal Spine: exit_code=101, duration_ms=4821                          │
│ Payload (Raw stdout/stderr):                                          │
│   "Compiling libc v0.2.147                                             │
│    Compiling syn v2.0.28                                               │
│    ... [14,800 lines of standard compilation output: ~1.2 MB] ...      │
│    error[E0308]: mismatched types in src/engine/buffer.rs:42:15        │
│    expected `usize`, found `u32`"                                      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

                                    │
                                    ▼ Selective Compaction Engine
COMPACTED EVENT RECORD (Warm/Cold Tiers):
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Turn: 42 | Event: TOOL_OBSERVATION | Tool: cargo_build                 │
│ Causal Spine: exit_code=101, duration_ms=4821                          │
│ Digest: "error[E0308]: mismatched types in src/engine/buffer.rs:42:15" │
│ Epistemic Metadata: head_lines=5, tail_lines=20, dropped_bytes=1258100 │
│ Cryptographic Attestation:                                            │
│   sha256: 4f3a9a7b9e11c8d6428e5f... [Authenticates raw execution]      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The causal spine consists of the formal event header: the turn index $t$, the unique trajectory identifier $\tau$, the timestamp, the model proposal $e_{\text{prop}}$, the supervisor authorization record $e_{\text{auth}}$, the tool action parameters $a_{\text{ext}}$, and the structural exit metadata (such as UNIX return codes, signaled exceptions, and execution duration). The causal spine is strictly immutable; it is preserved without modification across all storage tiers to guarantee that the agent's directional decision tree remains completely reconstructible.

Ephemeral observations, captured in $e_{\text{obs}}$, represent the physical outputs streamed back from the sandbox execution environment. During compaction from the Hot Tier to the Warm Tier, the runtime applies *epistemic pruning* to these observation payloads:

$$\Phi_{\text{compact}} = \left\langle \text{status}, \text{Head}(k), \text{Tail}(k), \text{Filter}_{\text{err}}(\text{stdout}), \text{SHA-256}(\Phi_{\text{raw}}) \right\rangle$$

Under this transformation, the compaction worker strips the vast internal expanse of the standard output stream, preserving only the first $k$ lines (to capture the execution invocation and environment headers), the final $k$ lines (to capture completion summaries or panics), and any lines matching domain-specific diagnostic filters (such as compiler errors, stack traces, or linter violations).

Crucially, the compaction worker computes a cryptographic digest $h = \text{SHA-256}(\Phi_{\text{raw}})$ of the original, uncompacted observation payload prior to truncation. This hash is permanently recorded alongside the pruned record. If an auditor, a security supervisor, or an automated evaluator later questions whether the summarized tool output genuinely reflected the sandboxed system's behavior, the runtime can verify any external copy of the original log against the immutable cryptographic digest stored in the trajectory's causal spine.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example: Storage Compaction Economics Across an Enterprise Fleet"}
Consider an enterprise agent cluster supporting $N = 2{,}500$ concurrent autonomous software development agents. Each agent executes an average of $T = 180$ turns per day.

*Baseline Parameters:*

- Model prompt context metadata: $S_{\text{prompt}} = 12\text{ KB}$ per turn.
- Model generation payload: $S_{\text{gen}} = 2\text{ KB}$ per turn.
- Tool invocation parameters: $S_{\text{call}} = 1\text{ KB}$ per turn.
- Raw tool observation output (compilers, git diffs, test runners): $S_{\text{obs}} = 350\text{ KB}$ per turn.
- Uncompacted event size: $S_{\text{turn}} = 12 + 2 + 1 + 350 = 365\text{ KB}$ per turn.

*Daily Ingestion Footprint:*

$$\text{Volume}_{\text{raw}} = 2{,}500 \times 180 \times 365\text{ KB} \approx 164.25\text{ GB/day} \approx 4.93\text{ TB/month}$$

Over a standard one-year compliance retention window, maintaining raw uncompacted logs requires $59.1\text{ TB}$ of capacity. When replicated threefold for high availability across distributed nodes, the infrastructure must provision $177.3\text{ TB}$ of high-IOPS block storage.

*Compacted Parameters (Hot-to-Warm Demotion after 24 Hours):*
The compaction engine applies epistemic pruning to $S_{\text{obs}}$. The runtime retains the exit code, a $4\text{ KB}$ extracted error trace, and a $32\text{ byte}$ SHA-256 digest:

$$S_{\text{obs, compact}} = 4.032\text{ KB}$$

$$S_{\text{turn, compact}} = 12 + 2 + 1 + 4.032 \approx 19.03\text{ KB}$$

*Compacted Footprint:*

$$\text{Volume}_{\text{compact}} = 2{,}500 \times 180 \times 19.03\text{ KB} \approx 8.56\text{ GB/day} \approx 256.8\text{ GB/month}$$

*Storage Compaction Ratio:*

$$\text{Ratio} = \frac{164.25\text{ GB/day}}{8.56\text{ GB/day}} \approx 19.19\times \text{ reduction } (94.8\% \text{ space savings})$$

When demoted to the Cold Tier after thirty days, the columnar Parquet representation with Zstandard compression achieves an additional $3.2\times$ compression factor on the structured text, shrinking the annual compliance archive from $59.1\text{ TB}$ to just $963\text{ GB}$. A single terabyte of cold object storage easily accommodates the entire corporate history of $164$ million autonomous operational turns.
:::

### Tombstoning, Cryptographic Shredding, and Retention Governance

While selective compaction prunes observation bulk, enterprise agent systems must also satisfy legal and regulatory mandates governing complete data lifecycle termination. Under statutes such as the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR Article 17) and corporate SOC 2 Type II controls, organizations must guarantee that sensitive user information, proprietary source code, and personally identifiable information (PII) processed by an agent are irreversibly erased upon user request or expiration of the retention window.

This requirement conflicts directly with the physical architecture of append-only, content-addressed storage. In an append-only log or an immutable columnar file on object storage, data cannot be modified in place. Rewriting multi-gigabyte Parquet partitions or running live compaction merges on distributed object stores to erase a single turn incurs catastrophic write amplification, degrades cluster read performance, and risks corrupting the causal integrity of adjacent trajectories.

Runtimes resolve this fundamental tension through two complementary systems mechanisms: logical *tombstoning* and physical *cryptographic shredding*.

```
ENCRYPTED TRAJECTORY PERSISTENCE WITH CRYPTO-SHREDDING:

Key Management Service (KMS)
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Master Key (KEK)                                       │
│   ├── Wrapped DEK (Trajectory τ_A) ──► [Active]        │
│   └── Wrapped DEK (Trajectory τ_B) ──► [SHREDDED / ZEROED]
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
Immutable Columnar Storage (Warm/Cold S3 Object Store)
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Partition: 2026-Q3-trajectories.parquet                │
│                                                        │
│ [Trajectory τ_A Record]                                │
│ Ciphertext: 8f4b2c... ──► Decrypts with DEK_A (Valid) │
│                                                        │
│ [Trajectory τ_B Record]                                │
│ Ciphertext: 3a9e1d... ──► Indistinguishable from noise │
│                           (DEK_B permanently destroyed)│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Logical tombstoning introduces a supervisory revocation record into the event stream. When an administrative command or user request demands the expungement of a trajectory $\tau$, the supervisor appends a signed tombstone event $e_{\text{tomb}} = \langle \tau, t_{\text{curr}}, \text{reason}, \text{auth\_sig} \rangle$ to the active log. During subsequent warm queries or trajectory reconstruction procedures, the storage layer inspects the tombstone registry; any trajectory marked with an authenticated tombstone is immediately filtered from query projections, rendering it invisible to evaluation pipelines and user-facing dashboards.

However, a logical tombstone merely masks the data; it does not satisfy strict regulatory mandates requiring the physical destruction of the underlying bits on disk. To achieve physical erasure without rewriting immutable archives, the runtime employs *cryptographic shredding* (also known as crypto-erasure).

Under this design, the runtime enforces an envelope encryption invariant across all storage tiers. When a new trajectory $\tau$ is initialized, the supervisor requests a unique, symmetric 256-bit Data Encryption Key ($\text{DEK}_\tau$) from an external Key Management Service (KMS). All event payloads, execution snapshots, and file diffs associated with trajectory $\tau$ are encrypted using $\text{DEK}_\tau$ (typically via authenticated AES-256-GCM) before they are dispatched to the storage engine:

$$C_t = \text{AES-GCM-Enc}(\text{DEK}_\tau, \text{Payload}_t)$$

The $\text{DEK}_\tau$ itself is stored within the KMS, protected by hardware security modules (HSMs) and access-control policies. The underlying immutable object storage records only the ciphertext $C_t$ and the unencrypted causal routing metadata (the trajectory ID and turn index).

When the retention horizon expires, or when an explicit right-to-be-forgotten deletion order is validated, the supervisor commands the KMS to permanently destroy the key $\text{DEK}_\tau$. Once the key is zeroed out in the HSM, the ciphertext blocks residing within the immutable Warm databases and Cold Parquet archives become mathematically indecipherable from random static entropy. The effective erasure of petabytes of distributed, immutable trajectory logs is accomplished instantaneously by destroying a single 32-byte key, entirely bypassing the need for expensive, high-amplification storage compaction rewrites.

Executing this multi-tier persistence strategy requires concrete software engines capable of coordinating append-only write paths, high-performance structured compaction, and archival serialization across heterogeneous hardware. How do systems engineers architect the underlying storage engines to satisfy these sub-millisecond logging requirements while simultaneously supporting analytical trajectory queries?

## Trajectory Storage Engines {#sec-vol3-persistence-engine-design}

When an autonomous agent runtime attempts to persist its execution history directly to a centralized relational database across a networked remote procedure call (RPC), transient network congestion or write lock contention injects tens of milliseconds of latency into the model's autoregressive decode loop. Because the supervisor cannot dispatch an authorized mutating tool action before its corresponding Write-Ahead Logging event $e_{\text{flush}}$ achieves non-volatile durability, synchronous network round-trips quickly become the primary throughput bottleneck for the entire host process. Conversely, buffering events in volatile host memory or relying exclusively on batched columnar formats such as Apache Parquet introduces a catastrophic durability hazard: an ungraceful process termination, kernel panic, or hardware preemption permanently destroys the uncommitted trajectory suffix, stranding the external environment in an unrecorded, non-recoverable state. Attempting to circumvent both hazards by writing to a standard embedded B-tree with synchronous disk flushes introduces destructive write amplification, where appending a small five-hundred-byte event record forces the underlying operating system to write an entire four-kilobyte or eight-kilobyte dirty page, rapidly exhausting the write endurance of non-volatile memory (NVMe) solid-state drives and triggering severe tail latency spikes during page splits.

**No single database architecture satisfies the conflicting physical requirements of trajectory persistence: sub-millisecond, append-only synchronous durability on the critical path of model execution; indexed, relational queryability for live operational debugging; and high-density columnar compression for petabyte-scale archival analytics. Production agent runtimes resolve this trilemma through a staged hybrid storage architecture, decoupling synchronous durability via local embedded log-structured merge-trees from asynchronous relational projection and batched columnar archival.**

::: {.column-margin}
The fundamental trade-off of trajectory persistence mirrors Stonebraker's classic observation: general-purpose database engines that attempt to handle transaction processing, low-latency logging, and analytical scanning within a single storage abstraction perform poorly across all three when subjected to extreme specialized workloads.
:::

### Storage Engine Primitives and Trade-Off Dynamics

The architectural requirements of trajectory storage diverge sharply from conventional transactional web workloads. A trajectory log is strictly append-only; historical events $e_i = (t, e_{\text{prop}}, e_{\text{auth}}, e_{\text{obs}})$ are never updated in place or reordered once authorized and flushed. Furthermore, persistence operations fall along two radically different latency boundaries. On the critical execution path, the supervisor requires a synchronous durability guarantee ($e_{\text{flush}}$) with sub-millisecond commit latency to minimize pipeline bubbles between the model's generation of an action proposal and the sandbox's dispatch of the external tool. Off the critical execution path, human operators and automated supervision monitors require indexed queries across thousands of concurrent trajectories to track error rates, inspect failure traces, or project current Agent Control Blocks ($\text{ACB}_t$), while downstream reinforcement learning pipelines require bulk, high-throughput sequential scans over billions of tokens of interaction history.
